Empirical Research Plan  

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: Panel shift–share instrumental-variables difference-in-differences (Bartik-IV-DID).  
Why appropriate?  
• County-year panel (1997-2009) gives rich time and cross-sectional variation.  
• “True” treatment—local supply‐driven change in small-business lending—is potentially endogenous to local demand conditions.  
• A Bartik-style instrument that interacts pre-crisis county lending shares (1996-1997 averages) with ex-post bank-level supply shocks isolates plausibly exogenous variation.  
• Including county and year fixed effects and, when studying the crisis, a post-2007 dummy creates a DID structure that nets out nationwide shocks and fixed local characteristics.  
Thus we obtain a causal effect of credit-supply contractions on employment in both crisis and normal times.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
Ti,t  = log(real CRA small-business loan originations) in county i in year t (or Δ log). A fall in Ti,t represents a credit-supply contraction.

Instrument (shift–share)  
Z i,t  = Σb  (Sharei,b,1996–97  ×  ΔS b,t ),  
where Sharei,b,1996–97 is bank b’s pre-crisis lending share in county i and ΔS b,t is the estimated supply-shift of bank b in year t (e.g., change in b’s loan-to-deposit ratio driven by wholesale funding stress).  

Control group / counterfactual  
Counties with low or zero pre-crisis exposure to banks that subsequently shrink credit supply serve as controls—they experience small (near-zero) predicted shocks.

Treatment timing  
• Crisis analysis: post = 2008–2009, pre = 2004–2007 (or full 1997–2007).  
• Normal-times analysis: use the entire 1997–2007 period; treatment varies continuously with Z i,t .  

No RDD, so no running variable/cutoff.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Relevance: Z i,t strongly predicts actual changes in county-level small-business lending.  
Plausibility: Likely—many counties are dominated by a handful of banks whose balance-sheet stress in 2008 was large and uneven.

A2. Exogenous shares: Pre-crisis bank shares are predetermined with respect to post-1997 shocks to employment.  
Plausibility: Shares are measured before the outcome window; banks did not choose 1996–97 county market presence based on knowledge of the future crisis.

A3. Exogenous shocks: Bank-level supply shifts ΔS b,t are orthogonal to county-specific labor-demand shocks, conditional on national year FE.  
Plausibility: ΔS b,t driven by bank funding problems (e.g., MBS write-downs) not tied to any single county.  

A4. Stable unit treatment value (no large cross-county spillovers).  
Plausibility: Reasonable—small firms mainly hire locally; labour markets are geographically segmented. Some spillovers likely but can be checked by excluding commuting-zone neighbors.

A5. Parallel trends (for DID framing): Absent the supply shock, employment in high- and low-exposure counties would have followed parallel paths.  
Plausibility: We can test by pre-period event‐study coefficients.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  

T1. Endogenous bank–county matching (shares not exogenous).  
Fix: (i) Use earliest possible shares (1996–97). (ii) Control for county pre-trends and observable 1990s covariates. (iii) Use leave-one-out Bartik (exclude bank b’s activity in county i when constructing its share).

T2. ΔS b,t may capture demand shocks in banks’ own core markets (e.g., Florida housing bust).  
Fix: Purge ΔS b,t using bank-level national exposures (e.g., losses on securities portfolios) rather than loan-performance metrics; include state-year fixed effects; run placebo on large-firm employment (should be less sensitive).

T3. General equilibrium spillovers across counties.  
Fix: Cluster standard errors at commuting-zone; drop large metro areas in robustness; show results similar when aggregated to CZ level.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional FE + IV
library(ggplot2)      # plots

# 1. Load data --------------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("county_panel_1997_2009.csv")   # assume tidy county-year panel

# 2. Variable construction --------------------------------------------------
# real lending (deflated) and log
dt[, log_lend := log(real_cra_smallbiz_loans + 1)]

# Instrument: shift–share variable already in file or build it
# dt[, pred_shock := …]

# Crisis dummy
dt[, post_crisis := (year >= 2008)]

# Employment outcomes
dt[, log_emp_small := log(emp_smallfirms)]
dt[, log_emp_total := log(emp_total)]

# 3. Main IV specification --------------------------------------------------
#   log employment on (instrumented) log lending, county & year FE
iv_main <- feols(log_emp_small ~ 1 | log_lend ~ pred_shock,
                 data = dt,
                 fixef = ~ fips + year,
                 cluster = ~ fips)
summary(iv_main)

# 4. First-stage F-statistic
summary(iv_main)$fs

# 5. Crisis DID variant -----------------------------------------------------
did <- feols(log_emp_small ~ high_exposure*post_crisis + county_covars |
             fips + year,
             data = dt,
             cluster = ~ fips)

# 6. Event-study pre-trend test --------------------------------------------
dt[, event_time := year - 2007]                # events relative to 2007
es <- feols(log_emp_small ~ i(event_time, high_exposure, ref = -1) |
            fips + year, data = dt, cluster = ~ fips)
iplot(es)

# 7. Robustness: leave-one-out Bartik --------------------------------------
dt[, share_looo := …]   # compute leaving county i out
dt[, pred_shock_looo := share_looo * bankshock]  # aggregate up
iv_looo <- feols(log_emp_small ~ 1 | log_lend ~ pred_shock_looo,
                 data = dt, fixef = ~ fips + year, cluster = ~ fips)
summary(iv_looo)
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  

Theory predicts that reduced credit supply constrains small-business hiring. I expect:  
• Crisis years: A 10 percent decline in real small-business lending lowers small-firm employment by roughly 2 percent (elasticity ≈ 0.2). Effects on overall county employment should be about one-third as large.  
• Normal times: Smaller but still significant elasticity, perhaps 0.05–0.1.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (shift–share IV)  

C1: Strong first stage (F>10) ................................................. 1  
C2: Shares predetermined and not affected by future shocks .................... 1  
C3: Shifters exogenous to county outcomes (exclusion restriction) ............ 0.5  
C4: Parallel trends / no differential pre-trends ............................. 0.5  
C5: Limited cross-county spillovers / SUTVA .................................. 0.5  
Total (out of 5) ............................................................. 3.5  

I judge the research design reasonably strong but not bullet-proof; credibility hinges on validating exogeneity of bank supply shocks and demonstrating no pre-trend differences.
